title: Orientation & Baseline: What "Advanced Reader" Means
goal: Understand the Level 7 finish line in concrete terms; take a baseline stamina/speed reading; meet the academic-vocabulary routine that runs through the whole level.

prompts: From Level 6: name the 5 expository text structures (sequence, cause/effect, compare/contrast, problem/solution, description) and the 4 reciprocal-teaching roles (predict, question, clarify, summarize). Write them from memory, then check against this list. If you can't recall 3+ of either, review your Level 6 notes before continuing — this level assumes both are automatic.

vocab.def: to work out something not directly stated, using clues plus what you already know
examples: The story never says she was angry, but I infer it from her slammed door.
Detectives infer who committed a crime from evidence, not confessions.
vocab.task: infer something about a neighbor from one clue (a locked gate, a light on at 3am) without being told it directly.

vocab.def: to confirm something using an independent, separate source
examples: One witness says the car was blue; a security camera corroborates it.
A single study rarely proves a drug works — later studies have to corroborate it.
vocab.task: name one thing you believe that is corroborated by more than one source (a news event, a fact from school), and one thing you believe that you've never checked against a second source.

vocab.def: a leaning toward one side, often invisible to the person who has it, that shapes what they notice, report, or leave out
examples: A company's own website has a bias toward praising its own product.
A sports fan's bias makes them see every close call against their team as unfair.
vocab.task: name a source (a person, a website, a channel) whose bias you already account for when you read or listen to it, and say what the bias is.

write.task: In 4–6 sentences: pick ONE of the four "rooms" you already do some version of in real life (you compare prices before buying something = data reading; you decide whether to trust a stranger's online review = source credibility) and describe, honestly, one specific time your instinct failed you — a time you believed something you shouldn't have. This is your personal baseline; you'll return to it in Session 14.

passages.title: The finish line, in a text
paragraphs: What Does It Mean to Read Well?

Ask a six-year-old what a good reader can do, and the answer is simple: read a page without stopping. Ask a hiring manager, a nurse reading a drug interaction chart, or a citizen deciding how to vote, and the answer gets larger and much harder to fake. Real advanced reading is not a single skill; it is a bundle of moves that specialists in different fields learned to make automatic inside their own subject before anyone called it "critical reading" at all.

A historian who opens a soldier's diary from 1770 does not read it the way she reads a modern newspaper. She asks who wrote it, when, and why, before she asks what it says — a soldier defending himself in court writes a different account than a bystander with nothing to lose. She then goes looking for a second, independent account of the same event, because a single voice, however sincere, is a claim, not a fact, until something else corroborates it.

A scientist reading a study asks a different set of questions: what, exactly, was measured; how many people or things were tested; and — the trap that catches almost everyone outside the field — whether two things moving together (say, ice cream sales and drowning deaths, both rising every summer) actually means one causes the other, or whether a hidden third factor (hot weather) is driving both. A journalist reading a company's press release asks who benefits if the reader believes the headline. A tenant reading a lease asks which sentence, buried in paragraph nine, quietly changes what a friendlier sentence in paragraph two seemed to promise.

None of these moves are exotic. They are teachable, and they are largely the same handful of questions — who is speaking, what is their evidence, does something independent confirm it, what would change my mind — asked inside four or five different rooms. Two large research traditions converge on this point from different directions. One (Shanahan & Shanahan, 2008) studied working historians, scientists, and mathematicians and found each discipline reads its own texts in genuinely different, learnable ways, and that generic "read the textbook" strategies stop working for readers once they pass roughly a middle-school level of skill. The other (the Stanford History Education Group's 2019 national study of nearly 3,500 students) found that most people, including capable ones, do not do this automatically online: over half judged a piece of unverified video "strong evidence," two-thirds could not tell a paid advertisement from a news story, and almost nobody checked who was behind a website before trusting it. The gap between those two findings is exactly what an advanced reader closes: not more reading, and not a longer checklist, but the specific, disciplined habit of asking a source what it is and what would confirm or break it, every single time, before believing what it says.

That is the finish line this level is built around: not reading faster, though speed matters, and not reading harder books for their own sake, though the books here are genuinely hard — but reading like the specialist whose room you happen to be standing in, and never fully trusting a single voice until something independent has had a chance to argue with it.
